docs.title: Spark Birds
docs.text:
Spark Birds is a production mobile birding application available on the Apple App Store. The system is built with Expo, React Native, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and Firebase/GCS-backed authentication and media storage. Its AI architecture combines computer vision, retrieval-augmented generation, ecological machine learning, and data-engineering pipelines with conventional transactional application services.

The current platform combines:

  • a protected REST API with layered backend services
  • a mobile client for browsing, prediction, community, analytics, and settings flows
  • a browser-based admin surface for moderation, support, species media, and promotions
  • a server-side image-identification pipeline
  • a retrieval-augmented AI Bird Log assistant grounded in species knowledge
  • a contextual bird-likelihood ML pipeline built from eBird/EBD evidence
  • spatially clustered nearby-bird alerts with per-user schedules, channel preferences, and durable email delivery
  • synced species galleries, calls, and songs
  • signed cloud media URLs returned by the backend
  • Firebase client-storage support for new prediction image and audio uploads
  • backend-driven promotions and operational workflow controls

docs.title: Core Features
docs.text:
• species catalogue and detail pages
  • prediction creation and editing
  • AI image identification with ranked suggestions
  • retrieval-augmented bird questions through the AI Bird Log
  • contextual bird-likelihood modelling with complete-checklist cohorts, deterministic hard-negative sampling, and reproducible model evaluation
  • resumable Stage 3 data backfills with checklist-boundary checkpoints and phase-level timing metrics
  • scheduled nearby-bird alerts using spatial clustering, Redis caching, species-level deduplication, and an idempotent email outbox
  • community sharing, ratings, reactions, and comments
  • moderation and support ticket workflows
  • backend-driven promotion cards after login
  • analytics over stored predictions
  • extra gallery images per species via bird_detail
  • species songs and calls resolved to signed Firebase/GCS URLs
  • prediction audio recording, upload, update, and playback

docs.title: Production And Model Notes
docs.text:
• image inference is server-side, not on-device
  • core product workflows now run against PostgreSQL in production
  • some ingestion and legacy helper tooling can still reference SQLite-oriented assets during the wider migration period
  • extra species images are still sourced from /uploads/birds/others_images locally, but migrated media is returned from signed Firebase/GCS URLs

  • xeno-canto import tooling is now part of the repo for filling missing species sounds

docs.title: Admin Web
docs.text:
The admin web is the browser-based administrative surface for Bird Platform.

In coding terms, it is a separate React + Vite client in admin-web/ that talks directly to FastAPI admin endpoints in bird-agent/main.py. It is used for four main jobs:

  • species media management
  • user feedback reply handling
  • community moderation case review
  • promotions management

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The admin web exists so that operational and moderation tasks do not need to be performed from the mobile app UI.

In coding terms, the older mobile admin review screens have been de-scoped and the browser admin is now the primary operational surface.

It gives admin users a larger browser-based control surface for:

  • finding a species quickly
  • reviewing all stored gallery images for that species
  • choosing the default species image
  • reordering or hiding gallery rows
  • assigning quality metadata to species images and canonical audio
  • reviewing user support messages
  • replying to users through the backend-backed feedback thread
  • reviewing moderation cases created from community reports
  • creating, previewing, updating, activating, and deleting promotions

docs.title: Runtime Shape
docs.text:
• frontend: admin-web/
  • stack: React, TypeScript, Vite
  • backend: FastAPI admin endpoints in bird-agent/main.py
  • auth: Firebase Auth sign-in on the client, Firebase ID token verification on the backend
  • data source of truth: backend database, not browser local state

There are two practical runtime modes:

  1. local/dev mode
  2. deployed production mode

In deployed environments, the admin UI and API can be served on separate hostnames while still sharing the same backend source of truth.

docs.title: Admin Views
docs.text:
The current admin web has three top-level views:

  • species
  • reports
  • promos

At a code level this is now modeled in admin-web/src/App.tsx as:

type AdminView = "species" | "reports" | "promos";

Inside reports, the admin first chooses one of four workflow lanes:

  • Comment / complaint
  • Report content
  • Report user
  • Block user

This makes the reports workspace the single entry point for support, moderation, trust and safety, and self-serve safety actions.

docs.title: Authentication Flow
docs.text:
The admin web signs the user in with Firebase Auth, then sends the Firebase ID token to the backend on each authenticated request.

High-level flow:

flowchart LR
    Admin["Admin user in browser"] --> UI["admin-web"]
    UI --> Firebase["Firebase Auth sign-in"]
    Firebase --> UI
    UI --> API["FastAPI admin endpoint + Bearer token"]
    API --> Auth["Backend token verification"]
    Auth --> DB["PostgreSQL-backed app database"]
    DB --> API
    API --> UI

Important behavior:

  • the backend still decides whether the authenticated user is an admin
  • non-admin or guest users are rejected from admin endpoints

docs.title: Promo Workspace
docs.text:
The Promos workspace is a browser-based operational surface for promotion management.

It allows admins to:

  • create a promotion row without writing SQL
  • edit all key fields used by the mobile app promotion flow
  • preview the card visually before saving
  • delete obsolete promotions cleanly

This is backed by the same PostgreSQL promotions table consumed by the app.

Typical editable fields include:

  • slug
  • title
  • body
  • image URL or bundled asset key
  • CTA label
  • CTA target
  • background color
  • active / inactive state
  • start and end timestamps
  • priority
  • display-after-login delay
  • repeat frequency

This admin workflow is especially useful for:

  • launch messaging
  • timed feature campaigns
  • image-only advert cards
  • testing and operational verification without direct DB access

docs.title: Promo Create / Edit Flow
docs.text:
At a high level, the promo workspace behaves like this:

flowchart LR
    A["Admin user"] --> B["Promos workspace form"]
    B --> C["POST/PATCH admin promotion API"]
    C --> D["FastAPI promotion service"]
    D --> E["PostgreSQL promotions table"]
    E --> D
    D --> C
    C --> F["Updated promo returned to browser"]

In public architecture terms:

  • the browser form owns draft state only
  • the backend remains the source of truth
  • the promotions table stores the promo definition itself
  • per-user delivery and cooldown behavior is tracked separately from the promo definition

docs.title: Promo Data Model
docs.text:
The promotions feature uses a split model:

  1. Promotion definition Stored as a backend record describing the card itself.
  2. Per-user interaction state Stored separately so the app can track whether a given user has already seen, dismissed, or clicked a promo.
flowchart TD
    A["Admin creates or edits promo"] --> B["Promotion definition"]
    B --> C["App can render this promo"]
    D["User sees / dismisses / clicks promo"] --> E["Per-user interaction state"]
    E --> F["Cooldown + audit behavior"]

This separation is useful because it lets the product team change campaign content without mixing that concern with user-level delivery telemetry.

docs.title: Ticketing And Safety Model
docs.text:
The admin and safety system works best when it is treated as four distinct flows rather than one generic ticket queue.

This documentation describes the intended operating model:

  • comment / complaint
  • report content
  • report user
  • block user

These flows have different risk levels, different automation, and different human-review requirements.

docs.title: Reports Workspace Model
docs.text:
When the admin enters Reports, they should not land directly in a mixed queue of unrelated case types.

Instead, the workspace starts with four clear choices:

flowchart TD
    A["Reports workspace"] --> B["Comment / complaint"]
    A --> C["Report content"]
    A --> D["Report user"]
    A --> E["Block user"]

    B --> B1["Support ticket path"]
    C --> C1["Content moderation path"]
    D --> D1["Trust & safety path"]
    E --> E1["Immediate self-serve block path"]

This is the interface model now reflected in the admin web.

docs.text:
The current browser admin now presents the reports area as a single wide Reports Workspace with:

docs.title: Lane purpose
docs.text:
• Comment / complaint This lane surfaces support-style user/admin conversation threads and agent replies.
  • Report content This lane handles post and comment moderation cases, including severity classification, binary outcome, and content-level actions.
  • Report user This lane handles account-level trust and safety cases, including enforcement actions and behavioural-signal review.
  • Block user This lane documents the immediate self-serve block behavior and its role as a safety signal, rather than treating it as a human review queue.

docs.title: Comment / Complaint Flow
docs.text:
Comment / complaint is the support lane rather than the moderation lane.

Key characteristics:

  • creates a support ticket
  • can pass through sentiment analysis or other prioritisation signals
  • requires a human agent response
  • remains open as a two-way conversation until the user is satisfied

This flow is best aligned with the feedback-style thread model, where the same underlying case can hold:

  • the original user message
  • the admin or support reply
  • follow-up conversation and resolution state

docs.title: Report Content Flow
docs.text:
Report content is the standard content moderation lane.

Key characteristics:

  • targets a specific piece of content
  • is auto-classified for severity before human review
  • still ends with a human moderation decision
  • has a binary case outcome:
  • action
  • no action
  • notifies both the reporter and the content author

This flow is narrower than trust-and-safety account review because the primary focus is the reported content item rather than the account's complete behavioural history.

In the current backend model, this lane now persists:

  • report_lane = report_content
  • auto-classified severity_label and severity_score
  • outcome = action_taken | no_action
  • optional content_action_type
  • notification timestamps for the reporter and the content owner

docs.title: Report Management UI
docs.text:
The reports workspace is evolving from a simple stacked review form into a report-management dashboard.

In coding terms, the moderation UI now maps the workflow model into a pipeline-oriented screen with:

  • stage columns that mirror the workflow:
  • New
  • Triaging
  • In review
  • Decision
  • Action
  • Closed
  • ticket cards that carry lane/type badges using the same visual language as the safety model:
  • comment
  • report content
  • report user
  • block
  • SLA state on each card so moderators can scan queue health quickly:
  • healthy
  • at risk
  • breached
  • a summary metrics bar at the top for:
  • open tickets
  • SLA at risk
  • SLA breached
  • closed today
  • multiple workspace views:
  • pipeline view
  • list view
  • analytics
  • a detail panel for the selected ticket showing:
  • ticket summary
  • reporter and subject user
  • priority and severity
  • lifecycle timeline
  • the currently active workflow action area

docs.title: Lifecycle timeline behavior
docs.text:
The detail panel mirrors the workflow diagram directly.

  • completed stages render as completed
  • the current stage renders as active
  • future stages render as pending

This allows the ticket detail panel to act as a live operational version of the workflow diagram rather than a separate UI concept.

docs.title: Stage-aware editing
docs.text:
Only the current actionable stage should be visible while the case is in progress.

In coding terms, this means:

  • future workflow sections should not be shown early
  • the card should expose only the current action area
  • once the case reaches notification_sent, it should be treated as resolved
  • resolved cards should collapse by default
  • resolved cards should show the notification state and offer a Re-open case action

This keeps the UI closer to a real moderation queue and avoids overwhelming moderators with fields that are not relevant yet.

docs.title: Report User Flow
docs.text:
Report user is the trust-and-safety lane.

Key characteristics:

  • more serious than reporting one content item
  • evaluates the user account more broadly
  • looks at account history and behavioural signals
  • supports escalating outcomes:
  • warn
  • temporary suspend
  • permanent ban

In the current backend model, this lane now persists:

  • report_lane = report_user
  • trust and safety actions in trust_safety_actions
  • derived behavioural signals in user_safety_signals
  • signal summaries returned to the admin UI for account-level review

This flow is better modeled as an account-level review rather than a single-post moderation ticket.

docs.title: Block User Flow
docs.text:
Block user is intentionally different from the ticket-based flows.

Key characteristics:

  • immediate self-serve action
  • no moderation queue
  • no human review step
  • no support ticket requirement
  • immediate effect for the blocking user

Even though it is silent from the user's perspective, the block event should still be logged as a safety signal so it can contribute to:

  • bad-actor detection
  • abuse heuristics
  • trust-and-safety model feedback

docs.title: Enforcement And Resolution
docs.text: Across these flows, enforcement and resolution are not the same thing.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
Enforcement actions include:

  • content action
  • warning
  • temporary suspension
  • permanent ban

These are intervention steps.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Resolution states include:

  • support conversation closed
  • moderation case resolved
  • trust-and-safety case resolved
  • silent user-level block completed

These indicate that the flow has reached an operational end state, whether or not enforcement occurred.

docs.title: Current Product Shape Versus Target Shape
docs.text:
The current product already separates some of these concerns, but the target model is broader and clearer:

  • feedback flows already exist and map naturally to comment / complaint
  • community moderation reports already exist and map naturally to report content
  • user-report handling exists, but the trust-and-safety lane should be treated as more account-centric than standard content moderation
  • user blocking already exists as an immediate self-serve action and should remain outside the human review queue

The main design improvement is to treat these as four distinct operating lanes rather than one shared ticket concept.

docs.title: How Species Media Management Works
docs.text: This is the core admin-web workflow today.

docs.title: Read flow
docs.text:
1. Admin signs in.
  2. Admin searches species with GET /admin/species.
  3. Admin selects a species.
  4. Admin web fetches the species payload and gallery rows with GET /admin/species/{species_id}/images.
  5. Backend returns:
  6. species identity
  7. default image
  8. ordered gallery rows
  9. canonical song/call audio URLs
  10. sound-quality metadata

docs.title: Edit flow
docs.text:
Inside the species manager, the admin can:

  • choose a new default image
  • move visible images up or down
  • hide an image from the gallery
  • restore a hidden image
  • adjust image_quality
  • adjust canonical song_audio_quality and call_audio_quality

docs.title: Save behavior
docs.text:
The admin web writes two separate concepts:

  • default image selection
  • gallery/image-quality ordering

Default image write:

  • PATCH /admin/species/{species_id}/default-image
  • backend updates bird_species.default_image_url

Gallery and image-quality write:

  • PATCH /admin/species/{species_id}/image-order
  • backend updates bird_detail.display_order
  • backend updates bird_detail.image_quality

Sound quality write:

  • PATCH /admin/species/{species_id}/sound-quality
  • backend updates bird_species.song_audio_quality
  • backend updates bird_species.call_audio_quality

docs.title: Hidden image rule
docs.text:
The admin web does not delete gallery rows when removing them from the visible gallery.

Instead:

  • visible rows use display_order = 0..N
  • hidden rows use display_order = 999

So Remove is really a hide operation, and Restore moves the row back into the visible ordered set.

docs.text:

    Search --> SpeciesAPI["GET /admin/species"]
    SpeciesAPI --> Select["Select species"]
    Select --> ImagesAPI["GET /admin/species/{id}/images"]

docs.title: Comment / Complaint Workflow
docs.text: The Comment / complaint lane is the admin side of the user support-message system.

docs.title: User flow
docs.text:
1. A signed-in user sends a support message from the app.
  2. Backend stores the ticket header in user_feedback.
  3. Backend stores the thread message in user_feedback_messages.
  4. That ticket becomes visible to admins through GET /admin/feedback.

docs.title: Admin flow
docs.text:
1. Admin opens Reports.
  2. Admin chooses Comment / complaint.
  3. Admin fetches feedback items through GET /admin/feedback.
  4. Admin writes a reply.
  5. Admin web submits PATCH /admin/feedback/{feedback_id}/reply.
  6. Backend updates:
  7. user_feedback_messages
  8. user_feedback.admin_response
  9. user_feedback.admin_user_id
  10. user_feedback.status = 'waiting_on_user'
  11. user_feedback.responded_at
  12. user_feedback.last_message_at
  13. The user later fetches the same ticket from the app and sees the response.

docs.title: User-close and stale-close behavior
docs.text:
The admin support lane should assume that support tickets are never hard-deleted from the database during normal user handling.

Instead:

  • a user may close their own ticket from the app, which sets user_feedback.status = 'closed_by_user'
  • the backend stale sweep may close waiting_on_user tickets after 7 days, which sets status = 'resolved'
  • both outcomes should remain visible as historical closed tickets rather than disappearing from audit history

docs.title: Key rule
docs.text:
The conversation is not stored as the main record on the phone and is not stored in Firebase as an application thread.

The source of truth is the backend ticket model in user_feedback plus user_feedback_messages.

docs.title: Moderation Workflow
docs.text: The Report content and Report user lanes are the admin side of community moderation and trust and safety review.

docs.title: User-side report creation
docs.text:
Users can report:

  • predictions
  • comments
  • users

Those actions create rows in community_reports.

docs.title: Admin-side review
docs.text:
The admin web loads moderation cases through GET /admin/community-reports.

Each report can include joined context from:

  • the reporter user
  • the reported user
  • the related prediction
  • the related comment
  • the admin reviewer

The current workflow is intentionally forward-only. In the current product shape, the admin moves a report through stages such as:

  • ticket_created
  • priority_triage
  • moderator_review
  • policy_decision
  • enforcement_action
  • notification_sent

The admin web writes updates through PATCH /admin/community-reports/{report_id}.

This updates moderation fields such as:

  • report_lane
  • workflow_stage
  • priority
  • severity_label
  • severity_score
  • outcome
  • content_action_type
  • admin_note
  • admin_reply
  • decision_note
  • enforcement_note
  • notification_message
  • reporter_notified_at
  • reported_user_notified_at
  • admin_user_id
  • reviewed_at

For Report user cases, the backend can also write:

  • trust_safety_actions
  • user_safety_signals

docs.title: Use case: admin manages a species gallery
docs.text:
1. Admin logs into the admin web.
  2. Admin searches for a species.
  3. Admin opens the species gallery manager.
  4. Admin reviews ordered image rows.
  5. Admin sets one row as default.
  6. Admin hides weak images or reorders visible images.
  7. Admin adjusts image and audio quality metadata.
  8. Backend persists the change.
  9. Mobile app and other backend-powered screens read the updated ordering/default image on the next fetch.

docs.title: Use case: user sends support feedback and admin replies
docs.text:
1. User submits a support message from the app.
  2. Backend stores the row in user_feedback.
  3. Admin opens the feedback view in admin web.
  4. Admin reads the message and replies.
  5. Backend stores the reply and the responding admin id.
  6. User later reopens support messages and sees the admin response.

docs.title: Use case: user reports community content and admin reviews it
docs.text:
1. User reports a post, comment, or user from the community experience.
  2. Backend stores a community_reports row.
  3. Admin opens Reports.
  4. Admin chooses either Report content or Report user.
  5. Admin reviews the joined context.
  6. Admin advances the workflow stage and records severity, outcome, trust-and-safety actions, moderation notes, and user-facing updates.
  7. The report remains part of the backend moderation record for later audit or follow-up.

docs.title: Read/Write Responsibilities
docs.text:
The admin web does not own business rules. The backend does.

The client is responsible for:

  • login initiation through Firebase
  • rendering admin views
  • sending structured update payloads

The backend is responsible for:

  • verifying Firebase identity
  • enforcing admin-only access
  • validating ordering and payload shape
  • resolving media paths into signed URLs
  • persisting updates into database tables

Examples of backend validation:

  • visible gallery orders must be contiguous starting at 0
  • hidden rows must use display_order = 999
  • image-order payload must include every image row exactly once
  • default image must belong to the selected species

docs.title: How Changes Affect the App
docs.text:
Admin-web changes are immediately important to the rest of the platform because the mobile app and API read the same backend data.

Examples:

  • changing bird_species.default_image_url changes species thumbnails and default detail images
  • changing bird_detail.display_order changes gallery order in detail screens
  • hiding rows removes them from visible gallery payloads while keeping them in the database
  • replying to feedback changes what the user sees in support-message history
  • updating moderation records changes admin review state for community cases

docs.title: AI Strategy
docs.text:
• inference is server-side
  • the backend can load either:
  • a reference-index artifact
  • a classifier artifact
  • sound training is now a multi-step pipeline:
  • ingest and top up clips
  • assemble a curated per-species dataset
  • train and save a .pt artifact for backend inference
  • mobile clients receive ranked predictions and confirm the final species choice
  • contextual likelihood training uses complete checklist events so present and absent labels share the same observation protocol
  • hard negatives are selected deterministically across local recency, local seasonality, and regional seasonality strata
  • long-running materialization jobs expose phase-level timings and resume only from fully committed checklist boundaries

docs.title: Artifacts, Embeddings, And Classification Flows
docs.text:
This page explains how the platform uses:

  • classifier artifacts
  • retrieval indexes
  • stored embeddings
  • RAG orchestration

It is intended to make the difference between:

  • bird-image-model.pt
  • bird-sound-model.pt
  • SQLite and manifest-based indexes
  • OpenAI embedding-backed retrieval

clear in one place.

docs.title: Classifier artifact
docs.text:
A classifier artifact is a saved trained model file that predicts a class label.

Current examples:

  • bird-agent/models/bird-image-model.pt
  • bird-agent/models/bird-sound-model.pt

These artifacts answer questions like:

  • "What bird is this image?"
  • "What bird is this recording?"

docs.title: Index
docs.text:
An index is a lookup structure used for retrieval rather than direct classification.

Current examples in this project:

  • SQLite tables such as bird_species, bird_detail, bird_species_sound_sources, and bird_species_rag_embeddings
  • training manifests such as gallery_sync_manifest.json and sound_training_manifest.json
  • local lexical retrieval structures built at runtime in bird-agent/rag.py

Indexes answer questions like:

  • "What recordings do we have for this species?"
  • "Which birds best match this question?"
  • "Which images belong to this training set?"

docs.title: Stored embeddings
docs.text:
Stored embeddings are saved numeric vectors representing text, images, or audio in a way that allows similarity search.

In the current repo, the main embedding-backed path is the optional OpenAI retrieval mode for bird Q&A:

  • embeddings are stored in bird_species_rag_embeddings
  • retrieval is orchestrated in bird-agent/rag.py

The project does not yet use a production vector index for image-identification or sound-identification inference. Those flows are currently classifier-first.

docs.title: Practical Reading Of The System Today
docs.text:
If the question is:

  • "What bird is in this photo?"
  • the answer comes from a classifier artifact

That is the core distinction between:

  • classifier artifacts
  • indexes
  • stored embeddings
  • RAG orchestration

docs.title: Backend Overview
docs.text:
The backend lives in bird-agent/ and now follows a much cleaner FastAPI structure than the earlier single-file main.py design.

The important architectural shift is:

  • bird-agent/main.py is now a thin ASGI entrypoint
  • bird-agent/app_factory.py is the application composition root
  • HTTP transport is split into routers by domain
  • business workflow is split into service modules
  • SQL access is split into repository modules
  • database bootstrap/schema/migration logic is split out of the web entrypoint

That means the backend now more closely follows the industry-standard Python layering:

  • router -> service -> repository
  • app_factory -> startup/lifespan orchestration
  • core -> config/constants/paths
  • app_db -> connection/schema/migrations/bootstrap

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text: The backend layers are intentionally strict.

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
Router modules are HTTP-only.

Their responsibilities are:

  • request params
  • auth dependency application
  • response shape
  • request model parsing through FastAPI/Pydantic
  • handing off work to the service layer

Router modules should not own:

  • SQL
  • workflow state transitions
  • transaction orchestration
  • non-trivial domain rules

docs.title: Service
docs.text:
Service modules own business behavior.

Their responsibilities are:

  • business rules
  • validation flow
  • workflow transitions
  • transaction orchestration
  • deciding which repository calls happen and in what order
  • coordinating shared helpers such as serializers, moderation helpers, and media cleanup

Service modules should not own:

  • raw SQL strings
  • route decorators
  • FastAPI dependency declarations

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Repository modules are persistence-only.

Their responsibilities are:

  • SQL only
  • fetch rows
  • update rows
  • insert rows
  • delete rows
  • aggregate queries
  • join queries

Repository modules should not own:

  • FastAPI concerns
  • HTTPException
  • auth logic
  • moderation workflow rules
  • prediction/community business decisions

This separation is now the core design rule for new backend work.

docs.text:
The repo now has two distinct Alembic migration trees and they do not own the same database.

  1. Main app database
  2. env var: DATABASE_URL
  3. production database name is typically bird_platform
  4. owns tables such as users, bird_species, predictions, community_reports, user_feedback, and trust_safety_actions

  5. Alembic config:

    • bird-agent/alembic-main-app.ini
    • bird-agent/alembic_main_app/

  6. Nearby alerts database

  7. env vars:
    • BIRD_ALERTS_DATABASE_URL
    • BIRD_ALERTS_DATABASE_URL_SYNC
  8. production database name is typically birdagent
  9. owns the nearby-alert scheduling/user tables only
  10. Alembic config:
    • bird-agent/alembic-nearby-bird-alerts.ini
    • bird-agent/alembic_nearby_bird_alerts/

Operational rule:

  • schema changes in the main product tables should go through the main-app Alembic tree
  • schema changes in nearby-alerts tables should go through the nearby-alerts Alembic tree
  • runtime bootstrap helpers in app_db/schema.py and app_db/migrations.py remain useful reference code, but production PostgreSQL schema evolution should now be handled through Alembic

docs.title: Full Test Harness
docs.text:
The current backend test harness is made of four cooperating parts:

In this codebase, the test harness means the full supporting test infrastructure around the actual test cases.

It is not just the test_*.py files.

It includes:

  • the pytest bootstrap and import setup
  • fake connections and in-memory databases
  • shared TestClient builders
  • dependency stubs for Firebase, media, and RAG imports
  • the conventions that let router, service, repository, and app-composition tests run reliably and independently

The purpose of the harness is to give each test layer the right execution environment:

  • router tests should feel like HTTP requests, not database tests
  • service tests should feel like business-rule tests, not Firebase or SQL integration tests
  • repository tests should execute real SQL, but only against small isolated temporary databases
  • app-composition tests should verify FastAPI wiring and lifecycle behavior without depending on live cloud services or model runtimes

So when we say “full test harness,” we mean the reusable Python testing infrastructure that makes the layered suite possible and stable.

docs.title: Bird Data Collection Pipeline
docs.text:
This page shows the end-to-end retrieval, augmentation, and generation flow used by the species metadata completion agent in bird-agent/bird_data_collection_agent.py, plus the one-at-a-time loop runners in:

  • bird-agent/run_next_bird_data_collection.py
  • bird-agent/run_bird_data_collection_loop.py

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: flowchart TD     A["60-second loop run_bird_data_collection_loop.py"] --> B["Run one species run_next_bird_data_collection.py"]     B --> C["Select next eligible row no_of_cleansing_passes = 0"]     C --> D["Retrieve trusted source text RSPB, eBird, BTO, All About Birds Wikipedia fallback"]     D --> E["Augment prompt species data + blank fields + source text"]     E --> F["Generate candidate JSON OpenAI extraction step"]     F --> G["Clean and validate fields"]     G --> H["Go / no-go gate"]     H -->|Write| I["Save only blank fields increment no_of_cleansing_passes"]     H -->|Ignore| J["Mark ignored set no_of_cleansing_passes = 100"]     I --> K["Update loop state"]     J --> K["Update loop state"]

docs.title: Decision Gate
docs.text: flowchart TD     A["Validated candidate fields"] --> B{"Trusted non-Wikipedia source?"}     B -->|No| C["Ignore source quality too weak"]     B -->|Yes| D{"Enough validated fields survive?"}     D -->|No| E["Ignore row is too thin"]     D -->|Yes| F{"More than 2 strong factual fields?"}     F -->|No| G["Ignore not enough strong facts"]     F -->|Yes| H["Write save missing fields only"]      H --> I["increment no_of_cleansing_passes += 1"]     C --> J["set no_of_cleansing_passes = 100"]     E --> J     G --> J

docs.title: Step Summary
docs.text:
1. The loop runner wakes every 60 seconds and starts one safe processing pass.
  2. The selector loads the next bird_species row where no_of_cleansing_passes = 0 and at least one target field is blank.
  3. The agent gathers trusted source text, preferring RSPB, eBird, BTO, and All About Birds, with Wikipedia only as fallback context.
  4. The OpenAI extraction step turns that context into candidate JSON field values.
  5. Cleaning and validation remove placeholders, wrong-shaped values, and weak field mappings.
  6. The gate decides write or ignore.
  7. A successful write fills only still-blank columns and increments no_of_cleansing_passes.
  8. An ignored row is marked with no_of_cleansing_passes = 100 so it is not selected again.

  • 100 row was reviewed and intentionally ignored, and should not be reselected

docs.title: Important rule
docs.text:
For each species:

  • the selected bird_species.default_image_url should also exist as one of that species’s bird_detail.image_url rows
  • admin reordering is stored in bird_detail.display_order
  • backend reads gallery images with:

  • is_managed = 1
  • managed_rank = 1..N
  • stale managed thumbnail rows are currently demoted to the end of the gallery instead of being deleted

That means:

  • bird_detail is the ordered gallery

docs.title: Likelihood And EBD Tables
docs.text:
These tables support the bird-likelihood pipeline and the additive EBD import path.

They are intentionally separate because they serve different jobs:

  • ebird_observations is the compact runtime evidence store used by the app
  • ebd_observations_raw is the richer near-raw landing table for bulk EBD extracts
  • bird_likelihood_training_examples is the materialized ML-ready feature/label table
  • bird_likelihood_models is the model registry

Used for:

  • recent historical density and recency features
  • compact serving-time bird occurrence context

docs.title: ebd_observations_raw
docs.text:
ebd_observations_raw is the additive near-raw monthly EBD landing table.

This table preserves checklist/event metadata that would be too heavy or too detailed for the compact runtime table.

It is primarily a staging, analytics, and offline-ML source table.

Column group Examples What it is used for Bird identity taxon_concept_id, common_name, scientific_name, subspecies columns Species identity and taxonomy joins Count / breeding / behavior observation_count_text, observation_count, breeding_code, behavior_code, age_sex Richer ecological and training features Geography country, state, county, iba_code, bcr_code, locality, latitude, longitude Spatial filtering and feature engineering Checklist metadata sampling_event_identifier, protocol_name, duration_minutes, effort_distance_km, number_observers, all_species_reported Complete-checklist negatives and effort-aware modeling Moderation / quality approved, reviewed, reason Filtering to trustworthy rows Comments / payload checklist_comments, species_comments, raw_payload_json Forensics, debugging, and future feature extraction Import lineage source_file, source_line_number, imported_at Traceability and reruns

Important columns:

  • global_unique_identifier uniquely identifies the raw row
  • all_species_reported tells us whether the checklist was complete
  • sampling_event_identifier groups rows by checklist/event
  • approved and reviewed help filter lower-trust records

Used for:

  • bulk EBD import storage
  • offline analytics
  • Stage 3 feature generation
  • checklist-aware negative example generation
  • re-materializing compact ebird_observations

docs.title: bird_likelihood_training_examples
docs.text:
bird_likelihood_training_examples stores materialized supervised-learning rows for Stage 3 bird-likelihood modeling.

Each row is an ML-ready example rather than a raw observation row.

Column Type Description id INTEGER Primary key source_observation_id INTEGER Linked compact source observation when available species_id INTEGER Foreign key to bird_species example_key TEXT Unique training example id label_present INTEGER Supervised target, 1 present or 0 absent split_bucket TEXT Dataset split such as train, validation, or test feature_version TEXT Feature-set version species_name TEXT Species label text observation_date TEXT Effective example date latitude REAL Feature latitude longitude REAL Feature longitude radius_km REAL Spatial aggregation radius lookback_days INTEGER Main lookback window recent_window_days INTEGER Recent evidence window historical_lookback_days INTEGER Long historical window ebird_sightings_count INTEGER Compact eBird evidence count community_sightings_count INTEGER Community evidence count user_sightings_count INTEGER User-specific evidence count recent_sightings_count INTEGER Recent sightings count nearest_sighting_km REAL Distance to nearest matching sighting last_seen_days_ago INTEGER Days since last matching sighting historical_month_matches INTEGER Same-season evidence count historical_total_matches INTEGER All-history evidence count season_score INTEGER Seasonal score Probability feature columns REAL Precomputed feature probabilities such as recent_probability, distance_probability, season_probability metadata_json TEXT Structured provenance and feature metadata created_at TEXT Timestamp updated_at TEXT Timestamp

Used for:

  • Stage 3 classifier training
  • evaluation / offline validation
  • model reproducibility by feature_version
  • checklist-aware positive/negative example materialization

For complete-checklist feature contracts, checklist identity is retained in the metadata payload. Deterministic sampling selects whole checklist events, and resumable backfills treat the presence of an already committed checklist identifier as a durable completion checkpoint.

The newer hard-negative contract records both its sampling contract and the selected ecological stratum. Candidate selection rotates deterministically across:

  • recent local presence;
  • historical local presence in the same season;
  • historical regional presence in the same season.

This produces more informative negative examples than arbitrary absent species while preserving reproducibility across reruns.

docs.title: Image Management Model
docs.text:
The current admin image-management model works like this:

  1. all manageable species images live in bird_detail
  2. image order is stored in bird_detail.display_order
  3. the selected default image is stored in bird_species.default_image_url
  4. the default image should be one of that species’s bird_detail.image_url values
  5. rows are never deleted just to hide them from the gallery UI

Current gallery visibility rule:

  • rows with display_order < 999 are treated as visible gallery images
  • rows with display_order = 999 are treated as hidden from the gallery
  • hidden rows still remain in bird_detail
  • hidden rows are still available in richer API payloads for future screens or admin tooling

Backend admin endpoints that operate on this model:

  • GET /admin/species
  • GET /admin/species/{species_id}/images
  • PATCH /admin/species/{species_id}/default-image
  • PATCH /admin/species/{species_id}/image-order

docs.title: Media Path Notes
docs.text:
• migrated species media is stored in the application database as stable storage paths instead of local /uploads/... URLs
  • the backend signs those paths at response time before returning them to the app or admin website
  • some older prediction rows may still contain already-signed cloud URLs, which the backend passes through as-is
  • predictions.audio_url is used by Add Prediction, Update Prediction, and prediction-detail playback flows

docs.title: Current Read Behavior
docs.text:
The app and admin website currently rely on these rules:

  • Bird List thumbnails use bird_species.default_image_url
  • Bird Detail hero image uses bird_species.default_image_url unless a prediction-specific image is present
  • community detail also prefers prediction-specific images first
  • Bird Detail gallery uses only visible bird_detail rows ordered by display_order
  • hidden gallery rows (display_order = 999) are excluded from additional_image_urls
  • richer image metadata is now also available via additional_image_items
  • the admin website edits:
  • bird_species.default_image_url
  • bird_detail.display_order

Admin-web gallery behavior:

  • Remove on an image row sets that row to the hidden-gallery state
  • Restore moves that row back into the visible ordered set
  • save writes:
  • contiguous 0..N orders for visible rows
  • 999 for hidden rows
  • this is a hide/unhide workflow, not a delete workflow

docs.title: Community Data Rules
docs.text:
• community state is layered on top of predictions, not stored as a separate post table
  • unsharing a prediction clears its community visibility flags without deleting the prediction row
  • deleting a prediction removes its attached community ratings, reactions, and comments
  • community rating/reaction/comment tables are only meaningful for predictions where shared_to_community = 1

docs.title: Bird Q&A Source Data
docs.text:
• bird_species is also the source table for the bird-question retrieval corpus
  • the new extended descriptive fields can improve local matching and OpenAI embedding quality when populated

docs.text:
The frontend is built with Expo, React Native, TypeScript, and Expo Router.

There is also a separate browser-based admin client in admin-web/ for Windows/macOS browser use.

In coding terms, the browser admin is now the official admin surface. The older in-app admin review screens have been de-scoped from the mobile app.

For screen-flow diagrams, use the split UI map pages:

  • Bird Detail View
  • Prediction Create And Update
  • Analytics And Community

  • customer image moderation is asynchronous, so a save with a newly selected image may take a short moment before the prediction is created or updated
  • the image picker helper under the add-prediction image tile uses a compact left-aligned Choose label with icon
  • iPhone keyboard support now uses a shared accessory with up, down, and tick actions on key form fields
  • tapping Identify dismisses keyboard focus before the AI request starts

docs.title: Community UX
docs.text:
• shared predictions are grouped by user
  • the signed-in user group is shown first
  • other users are ordered by highest average overall community rating, descending
  • each user group is collapsed to the latest shared card by default
  • tapping the chevron expands or collapses the rest of that user's cards
  • star-rating taps update the local card immediately without forcing a full feed reorder
  • broader feed ordering is refreshed on screen focus rather than during the rating tap itself
  • group headers show:
  • display name
  • {x} Birds sighted
  • Avg overall rating as stars
  • each card supports:
  • star rating
  • thumbs up/down reactions for non-owners only
  • comment count and a comments sheet
  • owner-only Delete action, which unshares the item from community but keeps the local prediction
  • non-owner report/block actions through an overflow menu
  • deleting the underlying prediction from Predictions removes it both locally and from Community

docs.title: Community Comments
docs.text:
• the comments icon opens a bottom sheet from the community card
  • the comment input auto-focuses on open
  • the sheet uses safe-area-aware sizing and keyboard avoidance for phone use
  • comments are listed newest first
  • adding a comment updates the local count immediately and persists centrally through the backend
  • long-press on another user’s comment exposes report/block actions

docs.title: Settings, Support, And Safety UX
docs.text:
• Settings now includes:
  • light / dark mode switching
  • Support messages for direct user-to-admin contact
  • Moderation case updates for report acknowledgements, admin updates, and user follow-up after a decision stage
  • account deletion
  • guest mode shows an inline login/upgrade path
  • guest-only restrictions are intercepted before navigation, keeping the user on the current bird-list screen while presenting a contextual sign-in prompt
  • guest sessions label the account action as Sign in rather than Log out
  • admin users see a handoff note that operational admin work now happens in the browser-based admin web
  • support tickets can be closed by the user and then move to Closed Cases instead of being deleted
  • reply actions now use clearer Reply wording in the support/moderation UI
  • resend-verification and related auth errors should fall back to user-friendly generic error text when no specific safe message is available

docs.title: Promotions UX
docs.text:
• promotions are backend-driven rather than hard-coded into the app
  • a promotion can be a CTA-driven card or a full-image advert card
  • display timing is controlled per promotion and can override environment defaults
  • repeat frequency is tracked per user through backend state
  • image-based advert cards can be shown as full-card creatives with only a dismiss control
  • promo configuration is now managed operationally from the browser-based admin web

docs.title: Bird Questions
docs.text:
• the Bird List header exposes a left-side bird icon
  • tapping it opens a top-drop question panel
  • the question input auto-focuses on open
  • the answer block can show the top matched bird image beside the answer text
  • the panel calls the backend bird-question endpoint and displays both the answer and best matching birds

docs.title: Analytics Map Behavior
docs.text:
• the map initially zooms to the densest cluster of prediction pins
  • a Show all pins control lets the user jump back to the full extent
  • map access from AI Bird Log remains on the current screen and prompts for an alert location when none has been saved
  • deleting an alert location clears the persisted coordinates as well as the visible field, preventing a removed location from reappearing after navigation
  • an empty required location field receives a green themed border so the next action is visually clear

docs.title: Nearby Alert Controls
docs.text:
• search radius, check interval, and sightings period use themed sliders
  • the selected interval and sightings-period values are displayed directly in their labels
  • supported check intervals include short polling choices through monthly checks
  • push and email channels use independent checkbox-style preferences
  • notification preferences and scheduling values are persisted through the backend alert profile

docs.title: API Integration
docs.text:
The app uses bearer tokens for protected routes and converts backend media paths into full URLs with getMediaUri(...).

For new prediction media, the frontend now prefers direct Firebase client uploads and falls back to backend upload endpoints when Firebase client configuration is unavailable.

Prediction-image moderation flow:

  • upload selected image to Firebase Storage
  • poll backend moderation status
  • save the prediction only after the image reaches approved
  • show rejection/error feedback when moderation fails

The admin website uses the backend admin endpoints directly:

  • GET /admin/species
  • GET /admin/species/{species_id}/images
  • PATCH /admin/species/{species_id}/default-image
  • PATCH /admin/species/{species_id}/image-order

The admin image manager now also exposes:

  • image_quality as a compact per-image numeric control
  • song_audio_quality and call_audio_quality as canonical A-E selectors
  • Remove / Restore controls for hiding gallery rows without deleting them

Blank or invalid image-quality values default back to 5.

There are now two practical admin-web modes:

  1. local/dev mode
  2. deployed Hetzner mode

Local/dev mode expects:

  • the Vite admin-web URL in the browser, for example http://<mac-ip>:4173
  • the FastAPI backend URL inside the login form, for example http://<mac-ip>:8000

Current deployed production shape:

  • https://admin.clevermatrixdevelopments.co.uk serves the built admin-web/dist
  • https://api.clevermatrixdevelopments.co.uk serves the FastAPI backend
  • the login screen is prefilled with the live API base URL

This keeps the admin UI and API on separate hostnames while the backend/database remains the source of truth.

docs.title: Media Rendering
docs.text:
• customer prediction image if available
  • otherwise species default image
  • gallery thumbnails for extra species images
  • gallery thumbnails exclude hidden rows where display_order = 999
  • richer image metadata can still be surfaced from additional_image_items even when an image is hidden from the gallery strip
  • species audio buttons using song_audio_url and call_audio_url
  • species preview audio duration is controlled by the Expo config/env setting rather than hard-coded timing
  • prediction audio playback using audio_url
  • Firebase/GCS signed URLs are treated as first-class image/audio sources
  • SafeImage resets internal loading/error state when the image source changes, which avoids stale blank tiles after prediction updates or uploads
  • the browser-based admin site updates default image selection and gallery ordering without relying on filename priority rules

docs.title: Git Workflow
docs.text:
This project uses a simple branch flow:

  • feature/... for active work
  • dev as the integration branch
  • main as the release branch

The recommended path is:

feature branch -> dev -> main

docs.title: 1. Start from dev
docs.text:
cd <path-to-bird-platform>
git checkout dev
git pull origin dev

docs.title: 2. Create a feature branch
docs.text:
git checkout -b feature/your-feature-name

Examples:

git checkout -b feature/prediction-audio
git checkout -b feature/firebase-client-storage
git checkout -b feature/bird-detail-notes

docs.title: 3. Make your changes
docs.text: Work normally in the feature branch.

docs.title: 4. Review before committing
docs.text:
git status
git diff

If relevant, also run checks such as:

cd bird-app
./node_modules/.bin/tsc --noEmit

or:

cd bird-agent
uv run python main.py

docs.title: 5. Commit the feature branch
docs.text:
git add .
git commit -m "feat: short description of the change"

Use the commit guide in contributing.md for message style.

docs.title: 6. Push the feature branch
docs.text: git push -u origin feature/your-feature-name

docs.title: Merge into dev
docs.text:
When the feature is ready:

git checkout dev
git pull origin dev
git merge --no-ff feature/your-feature-name -m "Merge feature/your-feature-name into dev"
git push origin dev

Test on dev before promoting to main.

docs.title: Merge dev into main
docs.text:
When dev is stable:

git checkout main
git pull origin main
git merge --no-ff dev -m "Merge dev into main"
git push origin main

docs.title: Delete the feature branch
docs.text:
After the branch has been merged:

git branch -d feature/your-feature-name
git push origin --delete feature/your-feature-name

If Git says the branch is not fully merged, only force delete if you are sure:

git branch -D feature/your-feature-name

docs.title: Before coding
docs.text:
• switch to dev
  • pull the latest origin/dev
  • create a new feature/... branch

docs.title: Before committing
docs.text:
• run git status
  • review git diff
  • run the relevant checks for app/backend/docs

docs.title: Before merging to dev
docs.text:
• commit everything on the feature branch
  • push the feature branch
  • switch to dev
  • pull origin/dev
  • merge feature into dev

docs.title: Before merging to main
docs.text:
• confirm dev is stable
  • switch to main
  • pull origin/main
  • merge dev into main
  • push origin/main

docs.title: After release
docs.text:
• optionally merge main back into dev if extra cleanup happened only on main
  • delete the old feature branch

docs.title: Short Solo-Developer Version
docs.text:
git checkout dev
git pull origin dev
git checkout -b feature/my-change

# make changes

git add .
git commit -m "feat: my change"
git push -u origin feature/my-change

git checkout dev
git pull origin dev
git merge --no-ff feature/my-change -m "Merge feature/my-change into dev"
git push origin dev

git checkout main
git pull origin main
git merge --no-ff dev -m "Merge dev into main"
git push origin main

docs.title: Notes for This Repo
docs.text:
• Start new work from dev, not main
  • Use non-interactive Git commands where possible
  • Prefer git merge ... -m "..." to avoid getting stuck in a terminal editor
  • Keep generated local reports out of commits unless they are intentionally part of documentation or reproducibility

docs.title: Image Ingestion Pipeline
docs.text:
This page documents the current image ingestion and image-training flow across Dropbox gallery imports, training dataset sync, and classifier training.

Key scripts:

  • bird-agent/prepare_dropbox_species_gallery_mapping.py
  • bird-agent/import_hd_bird_detail_images.py
  • bird-agent/ai/prepare_training_data.py
  • bird-agent/ai/download_commons_images.py
  • bird-agent/ai/download_inaturalist_images.py
  • bird-agent/ai/sync_training_images_from_gallery.py
  • bird-agent/sync_bird_detail_images.py
  • bird-agent/ai/train_bird_classifier.py
  • bird-agent/ai/bird_image_identifier.py

docs.title: End-to-End Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Dropbox gallery images<br/>legacy species folders"] --> B["Prepare Dropbox mapping<br/>prepare_dropbox_species_gallery_mapping.py"]
    B --> C["Import / migrate gallery images<br/>import_hd_bird_detail_images.py<br/>or Dropbox-to-Firebase migration"]
    C --> D["bird_detail table<br/>ordered gallery rows + provenance metadata"]
    D --> E["Species gallery in app/admin"]

    D --> F["Sync training images from gallery<br/>sync_training_images_from_gallery.py"]
    G["Reference/default images<br/>prepare_training_data.py"] --> H["Training dataset root"]
    I["Wikimedia Commons<br/>download_commons_images.py"] --> H
    J["iNaturalist<br/>download_inaturalist_images.py"] --> H
    F --> H

    H --> K["Audit + thresholding<br/>audit_training_data.py"]
    K --> L["Train classifier<br/>train_bird_classifier.py"]
    L --> M["bird-image-model.pt"]
    M --> N["Server-side image inference<br/>bird_image_identifier.py"]
    N --> O["POST /identify-bird-image"]
    O --> P["Mobile app suggestions"]

docs.title: Gallery And Training Relationship
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["bird_detail<br/>gallery order + provenance metadata"] --> B["User-facing gallery"]
    A --> C["Training sync"]
    C --> D["Per-species dataset folders"]
    D --> E["Classifier training"]

docs.title: 1. Species gallery images
docs.text:
The app-facing gallery is driven by:

  • bird_detail

Important fields:

  • bird_species_id
  • image_url
  • display_order
  • image_quality
  • source_name
  • source_record_id
  • managed_by
  • managed_rank
  • is_managed

Current meaning:

  • display_order controls gallery ordering
  • image_quality is training usefulness metadata, currently edited in the admin UI
  • source_name records the upstream source such as avicommons, wikimedia-commons, dropbox, or synced-gallery
  • source_record_id stores the source-specific identifier such as an Avicommons code:key pair or a filename/title
  • managed_by identifies the owning automation for refreshable rows
  • managed_rank stores the intended rank inside a managed gallery block
  • is_managed distinguishes automation-owned rows from legacy or manual rows

docs.title: 2. Training dataset
docs.text:
The classifier training dataset lives under a species-labeled root such as:

  • bird-agent/data/training
  • /Volumes/DATA/training

Expected structure:

training/
  1/
    species.json
    robin_001.jpg
    gallery_sync_manifest.json
  2/
    species.json
    blackbird_001.jpg

Each top-level folder name must match bird_species.id.

docs.title: A. Dropbox gallery import
docs.text:
Used for legacy gallery assets and migration work.

Primary steps:

  1. scan a Dropbox folder of bird images
  2. map filenames to bird_species.common_name
  3. generate cleaned filenames and storage paths
  4. review the mapping CSV
  5. import or migrate into gallery storage
  6. insert/update bird_detail

Main helper:

  • prepare_dropbox_species_gallery_mapping.py

docs.title: B. Gallery-to-training sync
docs.text:
Used to turn the species gallery into a classifier dataset snapshot.

Main helper:

  • sync_training_images_from_gallery.py

Current behavior:

  • reads ordered species gallery rows
  • downloads image files from the configured storage bucket
  • writes a local training dataset
  • writes gallery_sync_manifest.json per species
  • preserves provenance such as:
  • bird_detail_id
  • source_path
  • filename
  • display_order
  • image_quality

docs.title: C. External source enrichment
docs.text:
Used when a species needs more than the current gallery provides.

Helpers:

  • prepare_training_data.py
  • download_commons_images.py
  • download_inaturalist_images.py

Typical use:

  • seed every species with a reference/default image
  • add Commons or iNaturalist images
  • prioritize under-covered species

docs.title: D. Avicommons-first gallery refresh
docs.text:
Used to refresh the leading gallery block with traceable managed rows.

Main helper:

  • download_avicommons_thumbnails.py

Current behavior:

  • matches Avicommons records first
  • fills remaining slots from Wikimedia Commons quality-image categories
  • uploads selected thumbnails to Firebase Storage
  • inserts or updates bird_detail rows with explicit provenance:
  • source_name
  • source_record_id
  • managed_by = download_avicommons_thumbnails
  • managed_rank
  • is_managed = 1
  • pushes the current desired managed set to the front of display_order
  • demotes stale older managed thumbnails to the end instead of deleting them
flowchart TD
    A["Species id"] --> B["Match Avicommons records"]
    B --> C["Top up from Commons quality categories"]
    C --> D["Upload selected thumbnails to Firebase"]
    D --> E["Upsert managed bird_detail rows"]
    E --> F["Desired managed rows ordered first"]
    F --> G["Older stale managed rows demoted to end"]

Useful full-run command for one managed lead image per species:

cd bird-agent

.venv/bin/python -m ai.download_avicommons_thumbnails \
  --service-account "/absolute/path/to/service-account.json" \
  --bucket "bird_platform_1" \
  --all-species \
  --per-species 1 \
  --size 320

Useful progress checks while that run is in flight:

sqlite3 bird-agent/birds.db "
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bird_species) AS total_species,
  (SELECT COUNT(*)
   FROM bird_detail
   WHERE managed_by = 'download_avicommons_thumbnails'
     AND managed_rank = 1
     AND is_managed = 1) AS species_with_managed_lead_image;
"

sqlite3 bird-agent/birds.db "
SELECT
  totals.total_species,
  totals.completed_species,
  ROUND((totals.completed_species * 100.0) / totals.total_species, 1) AS percent_complete
FROM (
  SELECT
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bird_species) AS total_species,
    (SELECT COUNT(*)
     FROM bird_detail
     WHERE managed_by = 'download_avicommons_thumbnails'
       AND managed_rank = 1
       AND is_managed = 1) AS completed_species
) AS totals;
"

sqlite3 bird-agent/birds.db "
SELECT
  bs.id,
  bs.common_name
FROM bird_species bs
LEFT JOIN bird_detail bd
  ON bd.bird_species_id = bs.id
 AND bd.managed_by = 'download_avicommons_thumbnails'
 AND bd.managed_rank = 1
 AND bd.is_managed = 1
WHERE bd.id IS NULL
ORDER BY bs.id ASC;
"

Operational note:

  • the script currently prints only the final summary line
  • during the run it saves bird-agent/data/avicommons_thumbnail_manifest.json after each species, so that manifest file is the best non-SQL progress signal
  • summary.speciesProcessed is only finalized at the end, but the count of keys in manifest["species"] increases as species complete

Useful non-SQL manifest check:

cd bird-agent

python3 - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/avicommons_thumbnail_manifest.json")
payload = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
print("generatedAt:", payload.get("generatedAt"))
print("species entries:", len(payload.get("species", {})))
PY

docs.title: Training Flow
docs.text:
The image classifier training flow is:

  1. prepare a species-labeled dataset root
  2. ensure each class meets a minimum image threshold
  3. split images per species into train / val / test
  4. train the selected backbone
  5. save the artifact to:
  6. bird-image-model.pt

Current training script:

  • train_bird_classifier.py

Current inference helper:

  • bird_image_identifier.py

Current API:

  • POST /identify-bird-image

docs.title: Operational Notes
docs.text:
• The gallery and the training dataset are related, but not identical.
  • A good gallery image is not always a good classifier image.
  • image_quality is intended to help separate display suitability from training suitability.
  • Managed gallery rows are now tracked explicitly in bird_detail; filename conventions such as thumb_... are only a legacy fallback.
  • External drives and SMB shares can hold the training dataset, but local disk is still the most reliable option for model training.

docs.title: Current Status
docs.text:
What is already in place:

  • Dropbox-to-gallery mapping support
  • ordered species gallery in bird_detail
  • gallery-driven training sync
  • external-source enrichment scripts
  • image classifier training
  • saved image model artifact
  • backend image inference endpoint

What is still iterative:

  • dataset curation quality
  • per-species image depth
  • model selection and retraining cadence

docs.title: Community Moderation And Support Workflows
docs.text:
Spark Birds has two separate user-message systems:

  1. Community comments are public messages on community prediction posts.
  2. Settings/support feedback is a private support thread between a user and administrators.

These systems must stay separate in the code, database, admin screens, and documentation.

docs.title: 1. Community Comments And Public Post Interaction
docs.text:
Community comments belong to the public community feed. They are visible to users who can view the community prediction post.

flowchart TD
    A["User views community prediction post"] --> B{"User action"}

    B -->|Adds comment| C["Create community prediction comment"]
    C --> D["community_prediction_comments row created"]
    D --> E["Comment visible on community post"]

    B -->|Rates or reacts| F["Rating / reaction saved"]
    F --> G["Community post metrics updated"]

    B -->|Reports post| H["Create community report"]
    H --> I["community_reports row created<br/>target: prediction"]

    B -->|Reports comment| J["Create community report"]
    J --> K["community_reports row created<br/>target: comment"]

    B -->|Reports user| L["Create community report"]
    L --> M["community_reports row created<br/>target: user"]

    B -->|Blocks user| N["Create user block"]
    N --> O["user_blocks row created"]
    O --> P["Blocked user filtered from feed, comments, ratings, reactions, and future interactions"]

    I --> Q["Admin moderation workflow"]
    K --> Q
    M --> Q

docs.title: 2. Report Lane Classification
docs.text:
Community reports are grouped into lanes so the admin workspace can understand the type of case.

flowchart TD
    A["community_reports row"] --> B{"Report target"}

    B -->|prediction_id exists| C["Content lane"]
    B -->|comment_id exists| D["Content lane"]
    B -->|reported_user_id exists| E["User lane"]

    C --> F["report_lane = report_content"]
    D --> F
    E --> G["report_lane = report_user"]

    F --> H["Content moderation review"]
    G --> I["User behaviour / risk review"]

Content-lane reports cover reported posts and reported comments. User-lane reports cover reports about another user.

docs.title: 3. Admin Moderation Workflow
docs.text:
A community report moves through the admin moderation workflow. The internal workflow stage is more detailed than the user-facing status.

flowchart TD
    A["community_reports row created"] --> B["ticket_created"]
    B --> C["priority_triage"]
    C --> D["moderator_review"]
    D --> E["policy_decision"]
    E --> F{"Account enforcement needed?"}

    F -->|No| G["notification_sent"]
    F -->|Yes| H["enforcement_action"]

    H --> I["notification_sent"]
    G --> J["Reporter sees update in Settings"]
    I --> J

docs.title: Allowed stage transitions
docs.text:
The backend enforces strict workflow transitions so reports cannot skip required review steps unless a valid follow-up path applies.

Current stage Allowed next stage(s) ticket_created priority_triage priority_triage moderator_review moderator_review policy_decision policy_decision enforcement_action, notification_sent enforcement_action notification_sent notification_sent none through normal progression reporter_follow_up moderator_review, policy_decision, notification_sent

Important backend rules:

  • priority_triage requires a priority value.
  • moderator_review requires an admin reply.
  • policy_decision requires a decision note.
  • notification_sent requires a notification message.
  • Content-lane reports can use content_action_type but not trust and safety actions.
  • User-lane reports can use trust_safety_action_type but not content actions.

docs.title: User-facing status mapping
docs.text: Workflow stage User-facing status ticket_created open priority_triage open moderator_review reviewing policy_decision reviewing enforcement_action reviewing notification_sent resolved

docs.title: 4. Reporter Response Loop
docs.text:
After an admin response or final notification, the reporter may be allowed to respond.

flowchart TD
    A["Admin sends moderation update"] --> B["Reporter sees case update in Settings"]
    B --> C{"Can user respond?"}

    C -->|No| D["Case remains read-only"]
    C -->|Yes| E["User writes response"]
    E --> F["user_response saved on community_reports"]
    F --> G["user_responded_at timestamp saved"]
    G --> H["workflow_stage = reporter_follow_up"]
    H --> I["status = reviewing"]
    I --> J["Case returns to admin queue"]
    J --> K{"Admin next step"}
    K --> L["Admin moves case to moderator_review"]
    K --> M["Admin moves case to policy_decision"]
    K --> N["Admin closure from admin site"]
    N --> O["workflow_stage = notification_sent"]
    O --> P["status = resolved"]

This prevents user responses from disappearing. A reporter response should bring the case back to admin attention.

docs.title: Admin closure after reporter follow-up
docs.text:
If the reporter replies and no further investigation is needed, the admin does not have to replay the whole workflow from the beginning.

The admin may:

  1. move the case back to moderator_review
  2. move the case to policy_decision
  3. close directly from reporter_follow_up by setting workflow_stage = notification_sent

This direct admin closure path still requires a final notification_message, because the user needs a visible closing message in Settings and Closed Cases.

docs.title: 5. Content Actions
docs.text:
Content action is separate from user/account enforcement. A policy decision can affect the reported content, the reported user, both, or neither. The stored content_action_type decision can be content_removed, content_hidden, warning_only, or no_content_action.

flowchart TD
    A["Policy decision"] --> B{"Content action needed?"}

    B -->|Remove| C["content_removed"]
    B -->|Hide| D["content_hidden"]
    B -->|Warning only| E["warning_only"]
    B -->|No content action| F["no_content_action"]

    C --> G["content_action_type saved"]
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G

    G --> H["Decision note / admin reply saved"]

Expected content actions:

Action Meaning content_removed Content should no longer be available. content_hidden Content is hidden from normal users but may remain available for review/audit. warning_only Content remains visible, but the user receives a warning or guidance. no_content_action No content-level action is required.

docs.title: 6. Trust And Safety Actions
docs.text:
Trust and safety actions are account-level decisions. They are separate from content actions.

flowchart TD
    A["Policy decision"] --> B{"User/account action needed?"}

    B -->|Warn user| C["warn"]
    B -->|Temporary suspension| D["temporary_suspend"]
    B -->|Permanent ban| E["permanent_ban"]
    B -->|No user action| F["no_trust_action"]

    C --> G["trust_safety_action_type saved on report<br/>trust_safety_actions row created"]
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> H["trust_safety_action_type = no_trust_action<br/>No trust_safety_actions row created"]

    G --> I["Admin risk view updated"]
    I --> J["Notification prepared"]

Expected trust and safety actions:

Action Meaning warn User receives a warning but can continue using the app. temporary_suspend User is suspended for a limited period. permanent_ban User account is permanently banned. no_trust_action No account-level action is required.

docs.title: 7. Safety Signals
docs.text:
Safety signals are not the same as moderation cases. They are supporting risk indicators used by the admin to understand repeated behaviour.

flowchart TD
    A["User reports another user"] --> B["Safety signal logged<br/>source: user_report"]
    C["User blocks another user"] --> D["Safety signal logged<br/>source: user_block"]

    B --> E["Reported user risk view"]
    D --> E

    E --> F["Admin reviews risk history"]
    F --> G["Policy decision"]

Safety signals should help answer questions such as:

  • Has this user been reported before?
  • Has this user been blocked by several people?
  • Are reports isolated or repeated?
  • Is stronger trust and safety action needed?

docs.title: 8. Settings / Support Feedback Thread
docs.text:
Settings/support feedback is private. It does not create a community report unless the admin explicitly decides to escalate it.

flowchart TD
    A["User opens Settings / Support"] --> B["User submits feedback"]
    B --> C["user_feedback row created"]
    C --> D["Initial user message stored in user_feedback_messages"]
    D --> E["Status: waiting_on_admin"]

    E --> F["Admin sees ticket in feedback workspace"]
    F --> G["Admin replies"]
    G --> H["Admin message stored in user_feedback_messages"]
    H --> I["Status: waiting_on_user"]

    I --> J["User sees admin reply in Settings"]
    J --> K{"User next action"}

    K -->|Reply| L["POST /feedback/:id/messages"]
    L --> M["User message stored in user_feedback_messages"]
    M --> N["Status: waiting_on_admin"]
    N --> F

    K -->|Close| O["PATCH /feedback/:id/resolve"]
    O --> P1["Status: closed_by_user"]

docs.title: Nearby Bird Alerts Architecture
docs.text:
This page documents the eBird-powered nearby bird alerts module now integrated into the backend.

The selected interval controls when a user is eligible for another lookup. It is not a promise that an email or push notification will be sent at every interval: dispatch occurs only when the lookup finds a species code that is not already present in that user's seen-species history.

It is designed as a scalable sidecar domain inside bird-agent, with its own:

  • configuration
  • PostgreSQL tables
  • Redis-backed cache and task queue
  • Celery scheduler and workers
  • notification dispatcher

The current implementation lives in:

  • bird-agent/nearby_bird_alerts

docs.title: Radius Distance Math
docs.text:
The app filters all three nearby-map datasets against the saved alert center before rendering pins.

Inputs:

  • alert center:
  • lat1
  • lng1
  • sighting point:
  • lat2
  • lng2
  • selected radius:
  • radius_km

Decision rule:

  • include the point when:
  • distance_km <= radius_km
flowchart TD A["Saved alert centerlat1, lng1"] --> C["Calculate distance to sighting"] B["Sighting pointlat2, lng2"] --> C C --> D{"distance_km <= radius_km?"} D -- Yes --> E["Show pin on map"] D -- No --> F["Do not show pin"] sequenceDiagram participant Alert as Alert center participant Point as Sighting point participant Math as Haversine math participant Map as Map renderer Alert->>Math: lat1, lng1, radius_km Point->>Math: lat2, lng2 Math-->>Math: compute distance_km alt distance_km <= radius_km Math->>Map: include point else distance_km > radius_km Math->>Map: exclude point end

The current app uses the Haversine formula:

function toRadians(value: number) {
  return (value * Math.PI) / 180;
}

function getDistanceKm(
  fromLat: number,
  fromLng: number,
  toLat: number,
  toLng: number
) {
  const earthRadiusKm = 6371;
  const dLat = toRadians(toLat - fromLat);
  const dLng = toRadians(toLng - fromLng);
  const a =
    Math.sin(dLat / 2) * Math.sin(dLat / 2) +
    Math.cos(toRadians(fromLat)) *
      Math.cos(toRadians(toLat)) *
      Math.sin(dLng / 2) *
      Math.sin(dLng / 2);

  return earthRadiusKm * 2 * Math.atan2(Math.sqrt(a), Math.sqrt(1 - a));
}

This filter is applied to:

  • blue pins:
  • the logged-in user's app sightings
  • yellow pins:
  • other users' community-shared app sightings
  • green pins:
  • eBird nearby sightings

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The goal of this module is to notify users only when genuinely new nearby bird sightings appear for them, without making one eBird API call per user.

Instead, users are grouped into shared location clusters so the system can:

  • reduce external API calls
  • cache repeated lookups
  • diff results against each user's seen-species history
  • notify only the users who have newly relevant sightings

docs.title: Per-User Interval Throttling
docs.text:
The worker still wakes up globally, but it no longer processes every active user on every tick.

Instead:

  • each user stores:
  • check_interval
  • last_checked_at
  • next_check_at
  • the scheduler selects only users whose next_check_at is due
  • it immediately advances that due time before queueing cluster work
  • clustering then runs only across that due slice

This keeps the implementation efficient because the narrow sample happens in the database query before clustering and eBird fetches.

docs.text:
The clusterer groups users into shared grid cells using cluster_grid_degrees.

Why this matters:

docs.title: Notification Channels And Delivery Semantics
docs.text:
The dispatcher supports the destinations saved in the alert profile:

  • Expo push tokens use the Expo Push API;
  • other native push tokens use Firebase Cloud Messaging when server credentials are configured;
  • email uses Resend when selected by configuration, with SMTP available as an alternative;
  • webhook destinations receive an HTTP JSON payload.

Emails contain plain-text and HTML bodies. A successful provider API response means the provider accepted the request; it should not be interpreted as proof of final inbox or device delivery.

The implementation uses user_seen_species as its durable, per-user species deduplication record. This prevents a currently visible species from generating a notification on every scheduler pass.

Push and email preferences are stored independently. Push and webhook adapters remain immediate channel calls, while email uses a PostgreSQL-backed outbox:

  • discovery and email enqueueing commit together;
  • a content-derived unique key prevents duplicate email work;
  • the delivery worker claims pending or retryable rows in bounded batches;
  • network failures, HTTP 408, 429, and server errors receive exponential backoff, capped at one hour and five attempts;
  • non-retryable or exhausted failures are retained as permanent_failed;
  • successful provider acceptance stores the provider message identifier and acceptance timestamp.

This design preserves a clear distinction between a provider accepting a message and the message reaching an inbox. It also prevents a transient email provider failure from losing the underlying notification event.

docs.title: 4. eBird Client With Redis Cache
docs.text:
The eBird client performs cluster-level recent-sighting fetches and caches results in Redis.

Source:

  • bird-agent/nearby_bird_alerts/ebird.py

Current behavior:

  • cache key based on:
  • lat
  • lng
  • radius
  • days_back
  • max_results
  • default TTL:
  • 240 seconds

This avoids repeated eBird calls for the same cluster during a short interval.

docs.title: 5. Celery Beat And Worker Tasks
docs.text:
Source:

  • bird-agent/nearby_bird_alerts/tasks.py

Three main tasks drive the system:

  • schedule_all_clusters
  • Beat-triggered scheduler
  • check_cluster
  • worker task for one cluster
  • deliver_notification_outbox
  • worker task for due email deliveries and retries

Flow:

  1. Beat fires on the configured interval
  2. active users whose next_check_at is due are claimed from Postgres
  3. each claimed user's next due time is advanced from their saved interval
  4. due users are grouped into clusters
  5. one check_cluster task is queued per cluster
  6. each cluster lookup diffs against each user's seen history
  7. new species are persisted, enabled immediate channels are attempted, and email work is enqueued durably
  8. a separate worker delivers due email rows and records acceptance or retry state

Important scheduling note:

  • the app now saves a per-user check_interval choice with values:
  • 5m
  • 1h
  • daily
  • weekly
  • monthly
  • never
  • the backend API and Postgres model persist that value
  • Beat is still driven by the shared cadence from BIRD_ALERTS_POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS
  • the scheduler enforces each user's interval by selecting only due next_check_at values
  • never excludes the user from scheduled checks

docs.title: 6. Diff Engine
docs.text:
The diff engine is the core of the alert-value logic.

It compares:

  • the species currently present in a cluster
  • against each user's already-seen species set

Only the newly seen species are:

  • inserted into user_seen_species
  • sent to the notification dispatcher

This prevents noisy repeat notifications across poll cycles and restarts.

docs.title: 7. Notification Dispatcher
docs.text:
Source:

Supported channels:

  • push
  • email
  • webhook

The dispatcher only sends on channels that are configured and enabled for a given user. Email is invoked by the durable outbox worker; push and webhook delivery remain in the immediate cluster-processing path.
